name: base64-avx512 (Muła & Lemire)
baseline: base64 (conventional/table-based scalar base64 codec, e.g. Chromium's)
workload: Base64 encode/decode of buffers too large for L1 cache on an AVX-512 (VBMI) capable CPU
claimed_speedup: 10 to 20 times faster than a highly optimized conventional base64 codec (Chrome); AVX-512 codec reaches ~40 GB/s vs the conventional codec's 1.5 GB/s (encode) / 2.6 GB/s (decode); near-memcpy speed (up to ~150 GB/s for data fitting in L1)
hardware: Intel Cannon Lake (2018), 2.2 GHz (per paper Table 2)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 VBMI (Cannon Lake/Cascade Lake+); repo is the paper's artifact, not a general-purpose runtime-dispatching library; no fallback path bundled
caveats: Repo README has no numbers itself; the throughput/speedup figures come from the companion peer-reviewed paper (Software: Practice and Experience), not the bare repository page. Last commit is from 2019.

name: klauspost/crc32 (2025 AVX-512 revival)
baseline: CRC32 (Go standard library hash/crc32, IEEE polynomial - the same checksum family zlib's crc32() implements)
workload: IEEE CRC32 checksum of buffers from 512B to 32KB, aligned and unaligned, Go benchmark suite
claimed_speedup: 2.09x-2.35x faster than the prior (SSE4/AVX2) implementation for 1KB-32KB inputs using AVX-512; no speedup below ~1KB
tradeoffs: Go-only drop-in for hash/crc32; AVX-512 only engages above ~1KB inputs; CRC32C (Castagnoli) gains are noted as smaller and not worth the downsides per README
caveats: Comparison is against this same project's own prior (SSE4/AVX2) Go implementation of hash/crc32, not against zlib's C implementation directly; both sides implement IEEE CRC32, the same algorithm zlib's crc32() uses.

name: Chorba (table-less CRC32)
workload: CRC32 (IEEE) checksum of messages from 64KiB to 512MiB, 1000 iterations per size, on three platforms
claimed_speedup: Throughput of CRC32 increased by 100% (2x) across platforms compared with the current state of the art (zlib 1.3.1.1 braiding); on hardware-accelerated (PCLMUL / native CRC32 instruction) platforms the gain is 5-20% depending on message length
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 5600 (desktop); AWS EC2 t4g.micro (Graviton2/Neoverse-N1); Raspberry Pi 4
stars_or_usage: 6 stars; algorithm has been adopted by zlib-ng as the WITH_CRC32_CHORBA build option
tradeoffs: Table-less: trades lookup tables for extra registers/local variables; several polynomial variants selected by message-length range; some variants are destructive (modify the input buffer in place)
caveats: arXiv preprint (cs.DS), not confirmed to be published in a peer-reviewed venue; compiler and build flags are not stated in the paper (CPU/platform and iteration methodology are); the numeric results live in figures/graphs plus the abstract's summary sentence, not a full text table.

name: pybase64
workload: b64encode/b64decode of a 135,696-byte buffer, measured with the package's own 'pybase64 benchmark' CLI
claimed_speedup: b64encode: 17,492 MB/s vs stdlib base64.b64encode's 2,653 MB/s (~6.6x); b64decode: 9,037 MB/s vs stdlib base64.b64decode's 2,656 MB/s (~3.4x) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Python package with a C/SIMD (NEON/AVX2/AVX-512) extension; falls back to a pure binascii path if the compiled extension is unavailable; URL-safe (altchars) decode variants show smaller speedups (~2x) than plain decode (~3.4x)
caveats: Compared against Python's own stdlib base64 module (itself a thin C wrapper), not a C/C++ baseline directly; speedup varies a lot by variant/flag combination shown in the table.

name: const-hex
workload: Encoding/decoding byte buffers from 32 bytes to 1MB to/from hex strings, criterion 'cargo bench'
claimed_speedup: 10 to 50 times faster than the `hex` crate in encoding and decoding, and 100+ times faster than libstd's hex formatting; e.g. at 1MB, decode is 108,937 ns vs hex crate's 6,409,293 ns (~59x, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Rust-only; on x86/x86-64 performance is comparable to faster-hex, its main SIMD-based competitor, but const-hex is portable to other architectures where faster-hex has no SIMD path
caveats: Rust `hex` crate baseline, not a C/C++ implementation; benchmarks are reproducible via `cargo bench` but this session did not re-run them, only read the published numbers.

name: GaspardPetit SIMD base64
baseline: base64 (aklomp/base64, the reference SIMD-accelerated C99 base64 codec)
workload: Combined encode+decode of a 32 KiB payload, measured by the base64-benchmark harness across input sizes 32B-64KiB
claimed_speedup: 11.155 GB/s vs aklomp/base64's 9.118 GB/s (~1.22x) and Turbo-Base64's 10.206 GB/s (~1.09x) at 32 KiB on the Windows/MSVC run; also leads the Linux 32 KiB result (9.802 GB/s) and ranks #2 on macOS (7.179 GB/s), each measured on different hardware
compiler_and_flags: MSVC v19.51 (Visual Studio 2026, x64 Release) for the Windows numbers cited; Clang 20 (Linux) and Clang 21 (macOS) also tested
hardware: GitHub Actions hosted runners (windows-latest/ubuntu-latest/macos-latest); exact CPU model not published
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (new library); the benchmark repo that surfaced it has 117 stars
tradeoffs: Runtime-dispatched AVX2/NEON backend plus a slower portable fallback path; margin over #2/#3 (Turbo-Base64, aklomp/base64) is modest (~9-22%) and could be within noise for a different CPU/compiler
caveats: The benchmark repo and the winning library share the same author (gaspardpetit), a conflict-of-interest risk worth flagging; exact CPU model for the runs is not published (GitHub-hosted CI runners only); cross-platform throughput figures are explicitly noted by the author as not directly comparable since each OS ran on different hardware. Harvested as the top-ranked entry from the gaspardpetit/base64-benchmark shootout, which also confirms aklomp/base64 (already catalogued) and Turbo-Base64 (already catalogued) as the #3 and #2 performers respectively.
